etymology: From Old French deu, past participle of devoir, to owe, from Latin debere. Webster 1828: owed; that ought to be paid or done; proper; suitable; exact. In Scripture the great phrase is in due time — and it is God’s clock, not ours, that determines when due time has come.
biblical_def: Due in the Authorized Version most often appears in the phrases in due time and in due season, and both mean the appointed moment fixed by God. The greatest instance is Paul’s: when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly (Romans 5:6) — the incarnation and the cross did not happen when the world was ready but when God had determined, which Galatians calls the fulness of the time. The phrase then governs the Christian’s patience in three directions. In labour: let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not (Galatians 6:9). In humility under providence: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time (1 Peter 5:6) — the exalting is promised and its date is not. And in daily provision: The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season (Psalm 145:15), with the covenant version at Leviticus 26:4, I will give you rain in due season. The other sense of the word is obligation: give honour to whom honour is due, render therefore to all their dues, and the labourer’s wage is called his due in the same breath as his hire.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DUE as owed; that ought to be paid or done to another; proper; fit; appropriate; suitable; and, as a noun, that which is owed, or that which custom, office or law requires. Both the debt sense and the fitness sense are biblical.
webster_full: DUE, a. — Owed; that ought to be paid or done to another; as, a debt is due, a duty is due.
Proper; fit; appropriate; suitable; becoming; as, in due form, with due reverence.
Seasonable; as, in due time, at the proper or appointed season.
DUE, n. — That which is owed; debt; that which one contracts to pay, do or perform to another.
That which office, rank, station, social relations or established rules of right or decorum require to be given, paid or done; as, honour is his due (Romans 13:7).
scriptures: Romans 5:6
For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.
Galatians 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
1 Peter 5:6
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:
Psalm 145:15
The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season.
Leviticus 26:4
Then I will give you rain in due season, and the land shall yield her increase, and the trees of the field shall yield their fruit.
corruption_summary: An age formed by instant delivery has almost no category for in due time, and the result is a Christianity that treats delay as denial and reads every unanswered prayer as a refusal.
corruption_paragraphs: Every one of these texts assumes a gap. Galatians 6:9 says the reaping comes in due season if we faint not — the fainting is the danger, and the fainting happens in the gap. 1 Peter 5:6 tells a humbled man that God will exalt him and refuses to say when, and the very next verse tells him what to do meanwhile: casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you. Romans 5:6 supplies the pattern in the largest possible instance: four thousand years of promise between Eden and Bethlehem, and God called that moment due. A believer whose expectations are formed by immediate results will read providence as failure with monotonous regularity, and the only cure is the doctrine that the times are appointed.

The other sense of the word cuts against a different corruption. Romans 13:7 says, Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour — a verse that treats taxes, deference, and respect as debts rather than as favours a Christian may withhold when he disapproves. Paul wrote it under Nero. The same principle governs wages: the labourer’s hire is his due and not his employer’s generosity, and James pronounces woe on the man who keeps it back by fraud. Honour, money, and respect are owed, and a debt does not become optional because the creditor is unworthy.
roots_summary: Greek kairos (G2540), the appointed or opportune time, in the phrase in due time; opheile (G3782), a debt, at Romans 13:7; Hebrew eth (H6256), a set time.
roots_lines: Greek kairos (G2540) — a fixed or appointed season, as distinguished from chronos, duration; in due time (Romans 5:6).
Greek idios kairos — his own season; the phrase behind in due season we shall reap (Galatians 6:9).
Greek opheile (G3782) — a debt, that which is owed; render therefore to all their dues (Romans 13:7).
Hebrew eth (H6256) — time, season, the proper occasion; rain in due season (Leviticus 26:4).
Greek pleroma tou chronou — the fulness of the time (Galatians 4:4), the same idea stated of the incarnation.
usage: In due time Christ died for the ungodly (Romans 5:6) — the appointed hour of the greatest event in history.
In due season we shall reap, if we faint not (Galatians 6:9) — the promise, and the danger in the gap.
Thou givest them their meat in due season (Psalm 145:15) — providence keeping its own clock.

etymology: From Old English sceort. Webster 1828: not long; not extended in time or space; defective; deficient; not reaching the mark. The last sense is the one Paul uses in the most famous diagnostic sentence in Scripture: all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.
biblical_def: Short in the New Testament is chiefly a word of deficiency, of falling below a standard. Paul’s summary of the human condition uses it: For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23) — the Greek is in the present tense and means to lack, to be inferior to, to fall behind. It is not merely that men have committed acts; they are continually short of a glory they were made for. Hebrews applies the same figure to the danger of not entering God’s rest: Let us therefore fear, lest, a promise being left us of entering into his rest, any of you should seem to come short of it (Hebrews 4:1) — the wilderness generation stood at the border and fell short of the land. Paul uses it a third time in a hopeful sense of the Corinthians: ye come behind in no gift. And the word marks the compression of time in judgment and in mission: the LORD will make a short work upon the earth, and the time is short, so that they that have wives should be as though they had none. Prosperity is short, the days of man are short, and the devil’s time is short — having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SHORT as not long; not extended in time or in space; defective; deficient; not reaching a point or standard; and gives the phrase to come short for failing to attain or reach.
webster_full: SHORT, a. — Not long; not extended in length or in time; as a short journey, a short life.
Defective; deficient; not equal to a standard or measure; as, the sum falls short of what is required.
Not reaching a point or mark aimed at; as, the arrow fell short.
Scanty; insufficient; as, a short allowance; and, of temper, quick, sharp, or curt.
To come short — to fail; not to attain or reach; the exact phrase of Romans 3:23 and Hebrews 4:1.
scriptures: Romans 3:23
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
Hebrews 4:1
Let us therefore fear, lest, a promise being left us of entering into his rest, any of you should seem to come short of it.
Romans 3:22
Even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe: for there is no difference:
Romans 5:6
For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.
Revelation 12:12

Therefore rejoice, ye heavens, and ye that dwell in them. Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time.
corruption_summary: Romans 3:23 is quoted more than it is understood: the standard it names is not a moral average or a human ideal but the glory of God, and once that is seen, the comparisons by which men reassure themselves collapse.
corruption_paragraphs: The reason Romans 3:23 is so often heard as mild is that the standard is quietly replaced. If the mark is decency, most people clear it; if the mark is the average, half do by definition. Paul says the mark is the glory of God, and the verses immediately before have already dismantled every alternative: there is none righteous, no, not one, none that understandeth, none that seeketh after God, and every mouth stopped. The universality has no exceptions and no gradations, which is why the next verse can offer justification freely by his grace to exactly the same universal class. Take the standard down and the grace comes down with it; a small shortfall needs only a small remedy, and the cross becomes an overreaction.

Hebrews 4:1 puts the same word in the mouth of a pastor addressing a congregation, and the emotion he prescribes is fear. Let us therefore fear, lest… any of you should seem to come short of it. He has just recounted the wilderness generation who heard the promise, stood at the edge, and did not enter because of unbelief, and he applies it to people sitting in a Christian assembly. The Reformed doctrine of perseverance does not remove that fear; it explains how the fear works. God preserves His people through means, and one of the means is a warning that lands. A congregation that cannot be made to fear coming short has usually not understood what is on offer.
roots_summary: Greek hustereo (G5302), to come behind, to lack, to fall short; hustereo is also the verb of the prodigal who began to be in want; Hebrew qatsar (H7114), to be short or shortened.
roots_lines: Greek hustereo (G5302) — to come short, to be lacking, to be inferior; Romans 3:23, Hebrews 4:1, 12:15.
Greek doxa (G1391) — glory; the standard men fall short of in Romans 3:23.
Greek oligos (G3641) — little, small, brief; a short time (Revelation 12:12).
Greek sustello (G4958) — to draw together, to shorten; the time is short (1 Corinthians 7:29).
Hebrew qatsar (H7114) — to be short, to be shortened, to be impatient; the years of the wicked shall be shortened (Proverbs 10:27).
usage: All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23) — the standard is glory, not decency.
Lest… any of you should seem to come short of it (Hebrews 4:1) — a warning addressed to a church.
He knoweth that he hath but a short time (Revelation 12:12) — the devil’s rage explained by his calendar.

etymology: From Latin reservare, to keep back, to save up. Webster 1828: kept in store; retained; not delivered or given up. Peter uses it of an inheritance kept in heaven for believers, and of the unjust kept for the day of judgment — the same verb, two custodies.
biblical_def: Reserved is a word of custody, and Scripture uses it of two things being kept, one in hope and one in dread. Peter’s doxology gives the first: believers are begotten again unto a lively hope to an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4), and the next verse adds that they are kept by the power of God through faith — the inheritance is guarded for the heirs and the heirs are guarded for the inheritance. Nothing in that arrangement depends on the heir’s grip. The same apostle uses the word in the other direction: The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished (2 Peter 2:9). Jude says it of the fallen angels: the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day (Jude 1:6). And there is a third and lovely use, in Elijah’s despair: the LORD answers that He has reserved seven thousand in Israel who have not bowed to Baal, which Paul takes up in Romans 11 as the doctrine of the remnant according to the election of grace.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines RESERVE as to keep in store for future or other use; to withhold from present use for another purpose; to retain; and RESERVED as kept for another purpose, retained, not given up. The custodial sense is exactly Peter’s.
webster_full: RESERVE, v.t. — To keep in store for future or other use; to withhold from present use for another purpose.
To keep; to hold; to retain; as, to reserve a right or a portion.
RESERVED, pp. — Kept for another purpose; retained; not delivered or communicated.
RESERVED, a. — Restrained in words and actions; not free or frank — the modern conversational sense, absent from the Authorized Version.
From Latin re, back, and servare, to keep — the same verb behind preserve, conserve, and observe.
scriptures: 1 Peter 1:4
To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you,
2 Peter 2:9
The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished:
Jude 1:6
And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.
Romans 11:4
But what saith the answer of God unto him? I have reserved to myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to the image of Baal.
Romans 11:5
Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
corruption_summary: 1 Peter 1:4-5 is one of the strongest assurance texts in the New Testament, and it is weakened wherever the believer’s security is made to rest on the believer’s grip rather than on God’s keeping.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter states a double custody. The inheritance is reserved in heaven for you — out of reach of moth, rust, thief, and market — and the heirs are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation ready to be revealed in the last time. The word rendered kept is a military term for a garrisoned city. Both halves are needed and neither is the believer’s own work: he does not guard the inheritance and he does not garrison himself. This is why the Reformed doctrine of perseverance is more properly called preservation. The saints persevere, truly and actively, because God preserves them, and the faith through which they are kept is itself His gift. An assurance grounded anywhere else fluctuates with the weather of the soul.

Romans 11:4 shows the same reserving at work in a discouraged prophet’s crisis. Elijah, under the juniper, told God he was the only one left. God’s answer corrects the arithmetic and the theology at once: I have reserved to myself seven thousand men — not there happen to be seven thousand, but I have reserved, and to myself. Paul then draws the conclusion for his own generation: there is a remnant according to the election of grace. A believer who concludes from the visible state of the church that God has lost has made Elijah’s mistake, and the answer is the same. God keeps His own count, and He is the one doing the reserving.
roots_summary: Greek tereo (G5083), to keep, guard, reserve, in 1 Peter 1:4, 2 Peter 2:9, and Jude 6; phroureo (G5432), to garrison, in 1 Peter 1:5; kataleipo (G2641) at Romans 11:4.
roots_lines: Greek tereo (G5083) — to watch over, guard, keep, reserve; used of both the inheritance and the unjust.
Greek phroureo (G5432) — to garrison, to guard as with a military post; kept by the power of God (1 Peter 1:5).
Greek kleronomia (G2817) — an inheritance; the thing reserved in heaven.
Greek kataleipo (G2641) — to leave over, to reserve; I have reserved to myself seven thousand men (Romans 11:4).
Greek leimma (G3005) — a remnant; the conclusion Paul draws at Romans 11:5.
usage: An inheritance… reserved in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4) — the estate kept beyond the reach of loss.
To reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment (2 Peter 2:9) — the same custody, the opposite outcome.
I have reserved to myself seven thousand men (Romans 11:4) — God’s count against a prophet’s despair.

etymology: From Old English middel. Webster 1828: equally distant from the extremes; intervening; intermediate. The word’s great theological use is Paul’s middle wall of partition, the barrier in the temple court between Jew and Gentile, which he says Christ broke down.
biblical_def: Middle is fixed in Christian vocabulary by one phrase: he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us (Ephesians 2:14). The reference is almost certainly to the low stone barrier in the temple at Jerusalem which separated the court of the Gentiles from the inner courts, carrying inscriptions in Greek and Latin warning that any foreigner passing it had only himself to blame for his death. Paul, who had been accused of bringing a Greek past that wall and was nearly killed for it, writes from prison that Christ has demolished it. The chapter is exact about what was removed and how: the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances — the ceremonial partition of clean and unclean, circumcision and uncircumcision — abolished in his flesh, so as to make in Himself of twain one new man. The word appears elsewhere in ordinary senses: Samson took hold of the two middle pillars, and the veil of the temple was rent in the midst. But the middle wall is the one that decides how a church looks, because the two peoples were not reconciled by a compromise between them but by both being reconciled to God in one body by the cross.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MIDDLE as equally distant from the extremes; intervening; intermediate; and as a noun, the point or part equally distant from the extremities. The 1828 entry is purely spatial; the theological weight comes from Ephesians 2:14.
webster_full: MIDDLE, a. — Equally distant from the extremes; as the middle point of a line, the middle station of life.
Intervening; intermediate; occupying the place between others.
MIDDLE, n. — The point or part equally distant from the extremities.
Middle wall — a partition wall; the phrase of Ephesians 2:14, referring to the barrier of the temple court.
Josephus describes the temple balustrade and the inscriptions upon it forbidding Gentiles to pass, which is the background of Paul’s figure.
scriptures: Ephesians 2:14
For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;
Ephesians 2:15
Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;
Ephesians 2:16
And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby:
Galatians 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
Colossians 2:14
Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;
corruption_summary: Ephesians 2 and Galatians 3:28 are the two most abused unity texts in the New Testament, pressed to abolish distinctions Scripture maintains elsewhere — particularly the creational distinction of male and female and the ordered offices of the church.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul names exactly what was broken down: the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances — the ceremonial system that fenced Israel from the nations. That partition is gone, and any church that rebuilds it in another form, whether by ethnic preference or by cultural gatekeeping, is re-erecting what Christ demolished. What Paul does not say is that all distinctions whatever have been dissolved. In the same letter he addresses husbands and wives, parents and children, masters and servants, each in their own order, and he does it three chapters later. Galatians 3:28 is a statement about standing before God in justification — ye are all one in Christ Jesus, all Abraham’s seed, all heirs — not a denial that God made them male and female.

The egalitarian argument that Galatians 3:28 abolishes the created order proves far too much, since the same verse names bond and free, and no one supposes Paul meant that the household codes of Ephesians 6 were thereby cancelled — he wrote them afterward. The apostle who penned neither male nor female also penned 1 Timothy 2:12-13 and grounded it in the order of creation, not in culture. The right reading holds both: identical standing before God, and ordered relations within the household and the church. That is not a tension to be managed; it is the same structure the Trinity itself exhibits, equality of essence with order of relation.
roots_summary: Greek mesotoichon (G3320), a middle wall, joined with phragmos (G5418), a fence or partition, at Ephesians 2:14; mesos (G3319), middle.
roots_lines: Greek mesotoichon (G3320) — a middle wall; a hapax legomenon at Ephesians 2:14.
Greek phragmos (G5418) — a fence, hedge, partition; joined to the previous word in the same phrase.
Greek mesos (G3319) — middle, midst; the common adjective.
Greek echthra (G2189) — enmity, hostility; what the wall embodied and Christ slew (Ephesians 2:16).
Greek dogma (G1378) — a decree, ordinance; the law of commandments contained in ordinances (Ephesians 2:15).
usage: Hath broken down the middle wall of partition (Ephesians 2:14) — the temple barrier demolished in Christ’s flesh.
To make in himself of twain one new man (Ephesians 2:15) — not a compromise but a new creation.
Reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross (Ephesians 2:16) — peace with each other through peace with God.

etymology: From Old Norse leggr, a limb. Webster 1828: the limb of an animal used in supporting the body and in walking. Scripture gives the word two great uses — the legs God does not take pleasure in, and the legs of the Lamb that were not broken.
biblical_def: Legs in Scripture stand for the strength a man is tempted to trust. The psalm is explicit: He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man (Psalm 147:10), and the next verse gives what He does take pleasure in — them that fear him, in those that hope in his mercy. Cavalry and infantry, the two arms of ancient warfare, are dismissed in a line. The word’s most important occurrence is at the cross. To hasten death before the sabbath the soldiers broke the legs of the two thieves, but when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his legs (John 19:33), and John says this was done that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken — the Passover law that no bone of the lamb was to be broken, and the psalm which says the LORD keepeth all the bones of the righteous. The paschal lamb roasted whole in Exodus 12, legs and all, and the Lamb of God taken down whole from the cross, are the same picture. Daniel 2 gives a third use, the legs of iron in Nebuchadnezzar’s image, and the law required the legs of the burnt offering to be washed before they went on the altar.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LEG as the limb of an animal used in supporting the body and in walking and running; and notes its figurative use for support generally. Psalm 147:10 turns exactly on the figurative sense — legs as a nation’s military strength.
webster_full: LEG, n. — The limb of an animal, used in supporting the body and in walking and running.
The long or slender support of anything; as the leg of a table.
In Scripture, the legs of a man denote his strength or his speed; hence Psalm 147:10.
Exodus 12:9 and 29:17 require the legs of the paschal lamb and of the burnt offering to be dealt with in a prescribed way.
Song of Solomon 5:15 uses the figure of the Beloved: his legs are as pillars of marble, set upon sockets of fine gold.
scriptures: Psalm 147:10
He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man.
Psalm 147:11
The LORD taketh pleasure in them that fear him, in those that hope in his mercy.
John 19:33
But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his legs:
John 19:36
For these things were done, that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken.
Exodus 12:46
In one house shall it be eaten; thou shalt not carry forth ought of the flesh abroad out of the house; neither shall ye break a bone thereof.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Psalm 147:10 — that God takes no pleasure in the very capacities men are most anxious to develop, and takes pleasure instead in fear and hope.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Psalm 147:10 is one of the plainest verses in the Psalter and one of the least quoted, because it dismisses in a single line the two things every nation counts. The horse was the ancient world’s armour and the legs of a man its infantry; between them they are the whole military capacity of a kingdom. God says He takes no pleasure in either. The verse is not a criticism of strength as such — Scripture commends the strong man and the diligent hand — but a statement about what moves God’s delight, and the next verse names it: them that fear him, in those that hope in his mercy. Any church or family that measures itself chiefly by capacity has misread which verse it is living in.

John 19:33 is a piece of exact fulfilment that no participant intended. The soldiers were following a Roman practice and a Jewish request about the sabbath; the two thieves had their legs broken to hasten death; and Jesus, being dead already, was passed over. John, an eyewitness, says he records it that the reader might believe, and cites two Scriptures — the Passover rule that no bone of the lamb be broken, and the psalm that the LORD keepeth all the bones of the righteous. The providence that governed a soldier’s decision at a crucifixion is the same providence that governed Assyria and Babylon. Nothing about the death of Christ was left to the discretion of the men carrying it out.
roots_summary: Hebrew shoq (H7785), the leg or thigh, at Psalm 147:10; kera (H3767), the leg of an animal, in the sacrificial law; Greek skelos (G4628) at John 19:33.
roots_lines: Hebrew shoq (H7785) — the leg, the thigh; also the shoulder or heave offering given to the priest.
Hebrew kera (H3767) — the leg of a sacrificial animal; Exodus 12:9, 29:17, Leviticus 1:9.
Greek skelos (G4628) — the leg; only at John 19:31, 32, 33, all in the account of the crucifixion.
Greek katagnumi (G2608) — to break, to shatter; the verb of breaking the legs, and of the bruised reed He would not break.
Greek osteon (G3747) — a bone; a bone of him shall not be broken (John 19:36).
usage: He taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man (Psalm 147:10) — infantry and cavalry dismissed in one line.
They brake not his legs (John 19:33) — a Roman decision fulfilling a Passover statute.
Neither shall ye break a bone thereof (Exodus 12:46) — the rule the soldiers unknowingly kept.

etymology: From Old French requeste, from Latin requirere, to seek again, to require. Webster 1828: the expression of desire to some person for something to be granted or done; a petition. Scripture uses it of prayer — and once, terribly, of a prayer God granted.
biblical_def: Request is one of the New Testament’s words for prayer, and Paul’s use of it is the plainest instruction on anxiety in the epistles: Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God (Philippians 4:6), and the promised result is not that the requests are granted but that the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus. Four elements are prescribed — nothing excepted, prayer, supplication, thanksgiving — and the guarding is God’s answer whatever He does with the petition. Over against that stands the most sobering verse in Scripture about answered prayer: He gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul (Psalm 106:15). Israel lusted exceedingly in the wilderness and asked for flesh, and God gave them quails and a plague with them. It is possible to get what one asked for and be poorer. Ezra’s request from a pagan king was granted according to the hand of the LORD his God upon him, and Esther’s petition to Ahasuerus, at the risk of her life, was the turning of a nation’s fate. Requests in Scripture are made to kings and to the King, and both are answered by providence.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines REQUEST as an expression of desire to some person for something to be granted or done; a petition; and notes that request implies less urgency than entreaty and less authority than demand.
webster_full: REQUEST, n. — An expression of desire to some person for something to be granted or done; a petition.
The thing asked for or requested; as, he obtained his request.
A state of being desired or held in esteem; as, the commodity is in great request.
REQUEST, v.t. — To ask; to solicit; to express desire for; to entreat.
Webster notes that request implies less urgency than entreaty and less authority than a demand — a gradation Philippians 4:6 preserves by pairing prayer with supplication.
scriptures: Philippians 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
Philippians 4:7
And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
Psalm 106:15
And he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul.
Ezra 7:6

This Ezra went up from Babylon; and he was a ready scribe in the law of Moses, which the LORD God of Israel had given: and the king granted him all his request, according to the hand of the LORD his God upon him.
1 John 5:14
And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us:
corruption_summary: Psalm 106:15 is the verse that dismantles the whole apparatus of name-it-and-claim-it teaching: God can grant a request as a judgment, and the granting can leave the soul leaner than the refusal would have.
corruption_paragraphs: The wilderness generation asked for flesh, and the psalm says he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul. Numbers 11 records it: quails a day’s journey round the camp, and while the meat was yet between their teeth the wrath of God smote them. That single verse settles what the prosperity teachers cannot admit, that the granting of a petition is not proof of God’s favour and may be the form His displeasure takes. Romans 1 says the same in the language of judgment — God gave them up — and the most frightening thing a man can receive is exactly what he insisted on. This is why 1 John 5:14 attaches the promise to a condition: if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us.

Philippians 4:6-7 supplies the healthy pattern, and its structure is worth noticing. Paul forbids anxiety and then gives the alternative, which is not the suppression of the concern but its transfer: let your requests be made known unto God. Nothing is excluded — in every thing — and thanksgiving is required in the same breath, which is what keeps petition from becoming complaint. What is promised in return is not the granting of the request. It is a peace that will not be explained and a garrison round the heart and the mind. A believer may therefore come away from prayer with the matter unresolved and the anxiety gone, which is a stranger and better arrangement than getting what he asked for.
roots_summary: Greek aitema (G155), a thing asked, a petition; deesis (G1162), supplication; proseuche (G4335), prayer; Hebrew she’elah (H7596), a request or thing asked.
roots_lines: Greek aitema (G155) — a petition, a thing requested; Philippians 4:6, Luke 23:24, 1 John 5:15.
Greek proseuche (G4335) — prayer in general, always addressed to God.
Greek deesis (G1162) — supplication, a request arising out of need.
Greek phroureo (G5432) — to garrison; shall keep your hearts and minds (Philippians 4:7).
Hebrew she’elah (H7596) — a request, a petition, a thing asked; he gave them their request (Psalm 106:15).
usage: Let your requests be made known unto God (Philippians 4:6) — the transfer of anxiety, with thanksgiving.
He gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul (Psalm 106:15) — a granted prayer as judgment.
If we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us (1 John 5:14) — the condition attached to confidence.

etymology: From Latin determinare, to set a boundary or limit, from terminus, a boundary stone. Webster 1828: settled; concluded; fixed; resolved. The etymology is the doctrine: to determine a thing is to set its bounds, which is exactly what Acts 17:26 says God has done with the nations.
biblical_def: Determined in the New Testament is used of God’s eternal fixing of events and of a man’s settled resolve, and both belong in the same entry because Scripture puts them in the same book. Paul at Athens: God hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation (Acts 17:26) — not merely that nations exist, but their eras and their borders, fixed beforehand. Peter at Pentecost applies the same doctrine to the worst act in history: Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain (Acts 2:23). The crucifixion was determined, and the hands that performed it are called wicked in the same sentence; the church prayed the same thing in Acts 4, that Herod and Pilate and the Gentiles gathered for to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done. On the human side, Paul uses the word of his own resolve at Corinth: I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2) — a decision made in advance, against the appetite of a city that wanted wisdom.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DETERMINE as to fix the bounds of; to limit; to settle or decide; to resolve; and derives it from the Latin terminus, a boundary. The primary sense of setting bounds is the sense of Acts 17:26.
webster_full: DETERMINE, v.t. — To fix the bounds of; to limit; to bound; to confine.
To settle or decide; to end, as a controversy; to conclude.
To resolve; to fix a purpose in the mind; as, he determined to go.
DETERMINED, pp. — Ended; concluded; decided; limited; fixed; resolved.
From Latin de and terminus, a boundary or limit — the boundary stone, which is why to determine is first of all to set an edge.
scriptures: Acts 17:26
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
Acts 2:23
Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:
Acts 4:28
For to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done.
1 Corinthians 2:2
For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
Ephesians 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
corruption_summary: Acts 2:23 and 4:28 are the texts that make every attempt to soften the divine decree untenable: the crucifixion was determined before it happened, and the men who carried it out are called wicked for doing it.
corruption_paragraphs: Arminian and open-theist accounts of providence both work by loosening the decree — God foresees, or God responds, or God permits within a range. Peter’s sermon will not allow it. Christ was delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and in the same clause ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain. Acts 4:28 is if anything stronger, and it is a prayer: Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel gathered together to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done. The 1689 Confession states the doctrine in the only way the texts permit: God has decreed whatsoever comes to pass, yet so that neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creature. Both halves are asserted because Scripture asserts both.

The pastoral payoff is enormous and is the reason this doctrine belongs in the pulpit and not only in the classroom. If the worst act ever committed — the murder of the Son of God by religious and civil authority acting together — was determined beforehand and turned to the salvation of the world, then there is no evil in a believer’s life outside the same government. Joseph said it to his brothers, Paul said it in Romans 8:28, and the church in Acts 4 prayed it while under threat and then asked for boldness rather than deliverance. Paul’s own I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ is the human resolve that follows: a man whose confidence rests in a determined counsel can afford to preach an unpopular message.
roots_summary: Greek horizo (G3724), to mark out by boundaries, to determine — whence horizon; proorizo (G4309), to predetermine, predestinate; krino (G2919), to judge or decide, at 1 Corinthians 2:2.
roots_lines: Greek horizo (G3724) — to mark out with a boundary, to determine, to appoint; Acts 17:26, and of Christ declared to be the Son of God with power (Romans 1:4).
Greek horismenos — the participle at Acts 2:23, rendered determinate.
Greek proorizo (G4309) — to determine beforehand, to predestinate; Acts 4:28, Romans 8:29-30, Ephesians 1:5, 11.
Greek boule (G1012) — counsel, deliberate purpose; the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God.
Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, to decide, to resolve; I determined not to know any thing among you (1 Corinthians 2:2).
usage: Hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation (Acts 17:26) — nations bounded by decree.
By the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God… by wicked hands (Acts 2:23) — both halves in one sentence.
I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 2:2) — a preacher’s settled resolve.

etymology: Plural of calf, from Old English cealf. Webster 1828: the young of the cow. In Scripture the plural carries three distinct freights — the golden calves of Israel’s apostasy, the calves of the stall in Malachi’s promise, and Hosea’s startling calves of our lips.
biblical_def: Calves in the Authorized Version appear at the three great points of Israel’s worship, false and true. The apostate use is the most frequent: Jeroboam made two calves of gold and set one in Bethel and one in Dan, saying, behold thy gods, O Israel, and the sin of those calves is charged against every northern king thereafter. The sacrificial use is the ordinary one of the law, where bullocks and calves are brought to the altar. But Hosea, calling a ruined people back, replaces the animal with something else entirely: Take with you words, and turn to the LORD: say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips (Hosea 14:2). A people with no temple and no herds can still bring an offering, and the offering is confession and praise — a phrase Hebrews takes up as the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name. And Malachi ends the Old Testament with the third use, an image of released joy: unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall (Malachi 4:2) — stalled cattle turned out into the spring pasture, which is the last picture the Hebrew canon leaves with the reader.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CALF as the young of the cow, and notes the scriptural golden calf as an idol; the plural calves is also used of the fleshy part of the leg, an unrelated sense from a different root.
webster_full: CALF, n., plural CALVES — The young of the cow, or of the bovine genus of quadrupeds.
In Scripture, an idol; as the golden calf made at Sinai (Exodus 32) and the calves of Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:28).
The thick fleshy part of the leg below the knee — an unrelated word, from the Old Norse kalfi.
Calves of the stall (Malachi 4:2) — stalled cattle, fattened and confined, released to leap in the pasture.
Calves of our lips (Hosea 14:2) — a figure for the offering of praise and confession in place of animal sacrifice.
scriptures: Hosea 14:2
Take with you words, and turn to the LORD: say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips.
Malachi 4:2
But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.
Hebrews 13:15
By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name.
1 Kings 12:28

Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.
Psalm 51:17
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
corruption_summary: Jeroboam’s calves were not a repudiation of the LORD but a convenience — the true God worshipped in a form He had not commanded and at a location He had not chosen, which is the exact shape of most religious corruption since.
corruption_paragraphs: It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem is the whole argument, and it is an argument about convenience. Jeroboam did not tell Israel to abandon the God who brought them out of Egypt; he offered them that God nearer to hand, in a visible form, on a schedule he set, served by priests he appointed of the lowest of the people. Every element violates the second commandment and the regulative principle, and none of it required anyone to change gods. This is why the phrase the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin becomes the standing epitaph of the northern kings. Worship of the true God in a manner He has not appointed is not a lesser fault than idolatry; Scripture treats it as idolatry.

Hosea 14:2 gives the remedy and it costs nothing but everything. Take with you words — a people who had nothing left to bring, no temple, no herd, no standing, are told to bring words, and the words are given them: Take away all iniquity, and receive us graciously. The calves of the lips replace the calves of the stall, and Hebrews 13:15 makes this the church’s continual sacrifice. David had said the same from his own ruin: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. This is not a devaluing of sacrifice but its fulfilment, since the one Sacrifice has been offered and what remains for the redeemed is praise. And Malachi’s last picture says what such a people look like: stalled cattle let out into the sun.
roots_summary: Hebrew egel (H5695), a calf, and the feminine eglah; par (H6499), a young bull, in the sacrificial law; Greek moschos (G3448), a calf.
roots_lines: Hebrew egel (H5695) — a calf; the golden calf of Exodus 32 and the calves of Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:28).
Hebrew eglah (H5697) — a heifer; the red heifer of Numbers 19 and the figure of Ephraim as an heifer that is taught.
Hebrew par (H6499) — a young bull, a bullock; the chief sacrificial animal of the sin offering.
Hebrew marbeq (H4770) — a stall, a fattening pen; calves of the stall (Malachi 4:2).
Greek moschos (G3448) — a calf; the fatted calf of Luke 15:23 and the calves of Hebrews 9:12.
usage: So will we render the calves of our lips (Hosea 14:2) — praise offered by a people with nothing else to bring.
Ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall (Malachi 4:2) — the last image of the Hebrew canon.
Behold thy gods, O Israel (1 Kings 12:28) — the true God offered nearer, and in a form He forbade.

etymology: From Old English flowan. Webster 1828: to move along an inclined plane, as water; to issue or proceed from a source; to abound. Scripture uses it of the promised land, of the nations streaming to Zion, and of rivers of living water out of the believer’s belly.
biblical_def: Flow in Scripture is a word of abundance moving of its own weight. The land of promise is described from the burning bush onward as a land flowing with milk and honey, a phrase repeated some twenty times — the produce not merely present but running over. Isaiah turns the figure uphill, which is the point of it: it shall come to pass in the last days, that the mountain of the LORD’s house shall be established in the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow unto it (Isaiah 2:2). Water does not flow uphill, and Isaiah means that in the last days the nations will come to Zion against every natural expectation — a prophecy the church has watched being fulfilled for two thousand years. Joel promises that in that day the mountains shall drop down new wine, and the hills shall flow with milk. And our Lord takes the whole figure and puts it inside the believer: He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water (John 7:38), which John explains as the Spirit, not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified. The land flowed toward Israel; the nations flow toward the mountain; and the Spirit flows out of the believer.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FLOW as to move along an inclined plane or on descending ground, as water; to issue or proceed from a source; to abound, to have in abundance; and to melt or run, as metal. All but the last appear in Scripture.
webster_full: FLOW, v.i. — To move along an inclined plane, or on descending ground, as water; to run as a liquid.
To issue or proceed from a source; as, wealth flows from industry.
To abound; to have in abundance; as, a land flowing with milk and honey.
To rise, as the tide, opposed to ebb; and, of garments or hair, to hang loose and waving.
Webster’s third sense is the biblical idiom exactly: the land flows with milk and honey, meaning it abounds with them.
scriptures: Isaiah 2:2

And it shall come to pass in the last days, that the mountain of the LORD’S house shall be established in the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow unto it.
John 7:38
He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.
John 7:39
(But this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive: for the Holy Ghost was not yet given; because that Jesus was not yet glorified.)
Exodus 3:8

And I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up out of that land unto a good land and a large, unto a land flowing with milk and honey; unto the place of the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
Joel 3:18

And it shall come to pass in that day, that the mountains shall drop down new wine, and the hills shall flow with milk, and all the rivers of Judah shall flow with waters, and a fountain shall come forth of the house of the LORD, and shall water the valley of Shittim.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 2:2 is claimed by dispensational schemes as a millennial arrangement still wholly future, and by liberal readings as a poetic hope for universal brotherhood; the New Testament reads it as being fulfilled in the ingathering of the Gentiles into the church.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase in the last days is the hinge, and the New Testament defines it. Peter at Pentecost quotes Joel’s it shall come to pass in the last days and says this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel; Hebrews opens with God… hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son; John says it is the last time. The last days began with the first advent. Isaiah 2 is therefore being fulfilled now, as the nations come to the mountain of the LORD’s house — which Hebrews 12 identifies as mount Sion, the heavenly Jerusalem, the general assembly and church of the firstborn. Postponing the whole prophecy to a future earthly millennium removes it from the church’s present hope and mission, and the liberal reading empties it of the God who is doing the gathering.

John 7:38 needs care in the opposite direction, because it is a favourite of the charismatic movement and is regularly detached from what John himself says about it. Christ promises rivers of living water flowing out of the believer, and John adds the inspired explanation in the next verse: this spake he of the Spirit, which they that believe on him should receive, and it awaited the glorification of Christ. The promise is fulfilled to every believer at conversion, not to a second class of Christians at a later crisis; Romans 8:9 says if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of His. What the passage promises is an overflow toward others, and the shape of it is given in Galatians 5 as fruit rather than as sensation.
roots_summary: Hebrew nahar (H5102), to flow or stream, and by figure to shine; zub (H2100), to flow or gush, in flowing with milk and honey; Greek rheo (G4482), to flow.
roots_lines: Hebrew nahar (H5102) — to flow, to stream together; all nations shall flow unto it (Isaiah 2:2), from nahar, a river.
Hebrew zub (H2100) — to flow, to gush, to issue; the participle in a land flowing with milk and honey.
Hebrew chalab (H2461) and debash (H1706) — milk and honey; pastoral and wild produce together, the two signs of a good land.
Greek rheo (G4482) — to flow, to run as water; a hapax legomenon at John 7:38.
Greek potamos (G4215) — a river, a torrent; rivers of living water in the same verse.
usage: All nations shall flow unto it (Isaiah 2:2) — the nations moving uphill, against nature.
Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water (John 7:38) — explained by John as the Spirit.
A land flowing with milk and honey (Exodus 3:8) — abundance running over, promised at the bush.

etymology: From horse and man. Webster 1828: a rider on horseback; a man skilled in riding; and, in the plural, cavalry, mounted troops. In Scripture horsemen are the arm of war a nation is most tempted to trust, and the title Elisha gave to a single praying prophet.
biblical_def: Horsemen are the cavalry, the fastest and most feared arm of ancient war, and Scripture uses them chiefly to expose misplaced confidence. Pharaoh’s horses and chariots… and his horsemen, and his army pursued Israel to the sea and drowned there (Exodus 14:9). Isaiah pronounces the woe: Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD! (Isaiah 31:1). The indictment is not that horsemen are useless but that Judah looked to them and not to God. The psalm states the alternative in a line every believer should know: Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God (Psalm 20:7). Then comes the reversal that gives the word its glory. As Elijah went up in the whirlwind, Elisha cried, My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof (2 Kings 2:12) — the real cavalry of the nation was one man who prayed. The same words were spoken over Elisha’s own deathbed by the king (2 Kings 13:14). And his servant, hemmed in at Dothan, was shown the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HORSEMAN as a rider on horseback; a man skilled in riding; and a mounted soldier — the plural denoting cavalry. The military sense is the biblical one throughout.
webster_full: HORSEMAN, n. — A rider on horseback; one who is skilled in riding.
A mounted soldier; a trooper; in the plural, cavalry.
HORSEMANSHIP, n. — The act or art of riding, and of training and managing horses.
The law forbade the king of Israel to multiply horses to himself, nor cause the people to return to Egypt to that end (Deuteronomy 17:16).
That prohibition is the background to Isaiah 31:1 and to Solomon’s importation of horses from Egypt in 1 Kings 10:28-29.
scriptures: Exodus 14:9
But the Egyptians pursued after them, all the horses and chariots of Pharaoh, and his horsemen, and his army, and overtook them encamping by the sea, beside Pihahiroth, before Baalzephon.
Isaiah 31:1

Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD!
Psalm 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
2 Kings 2:12
And Elisha saw it, and he cried, My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof. And he saw him no more: and he took hold of his own clothes, and rent them in two pieces.
2 Kings 6:17

And Elisha prayed, and said, LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 31:1 is not a warning against armies but against the direction of a nation’s gaze, and the modern equivalents — the reserves, the platform, the institution, the plan — produce exactly the same woe.
corruption_paragraphs: Judah’s error was not that she armed but that she went down to Egypt for help and did not look unto the Holy One of Israel. Isaiah’s indictment turns entirely on the last clause: they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD. The horses and chariots were real, the Egyptians were genuinely strong, and the whole calculation was sound in every respect except the one that mattered. Scripture never treats prudence as sin — Nehemiah set a watch and prayed, and the law regulated an army. What it forbids is the transfer of trust, and the transfer is nearly always invisible, because the outward arrangements of the faithless and the faithful look almost identical. Psalm 20:7 gives the test: what does a man remember when the day of battle comes.

Elisha’s cry supplies the doctrine positively and should be preached where the church is anxious about its strength. My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof — the nation’s real defence, in the prophet’s estimate, was the old man being carried up in the whirlwind, not the standing army of the northern kingdom. A generation later the king of Israel wept the identical words over Elisha’s deathbed. And when the Syrian host surrounded Dothan and the servant despaired, the prophet prayed and the young man saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. The invisible cavalry was always there. What the servant needed was not reinforcements but opened eyes.
roots_summary: Hebrew parash (H6571), a horseman or a horse for riding; sus (H5483), a horse; rekeb (H7393), a chariot; Greek hippeus (G2460), a horseman.
roots_lines: Hebrew parash (H6571) — a horseman, a rider; also used of the horse itself in some passages.
Hebrew sus (H5483) — a horse; some trust in chariots, and some in horses (Psalm 20:7).
Hebrew rekeb (H7393) — a chariot, or chariotry collectively; Elisha’s chariot of Israel.
Hebrew Qadosh Yisrael — the Holy One of Israel; Isaiah’s characteristic title for God, used thirty times in his book.
Greek hippeus (G2460) — a horseman; Acts 23:23, 32, of the escort that took Paul to Caesarea.
usage: Trust in chariots… and in horsemen, because they are very strong (Isaiah 31:1) — a sound calculation with God omitted.
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember (Psalm 20:7) — the test is what a man remembers.
The chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof (2 Kings 2:12) — a nation’s real cavalry was one praying man.
